# Appeal of Denial — Total Hip Replacement (CPT 27130)

**RE: Notice of Adverse Benefit Determination dated 2026-07-31**
**Member:** Morgan Iverson
**Member ID:** W702529422
**Reference Number:** POC-1C4D453F27-72744
**Governing Policy:** Surgery of the Hip (2026T0503JJ), UnitedHealthcare, effective March 1, 2026 — https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/policies/comm-medical-drug/surgery-hip.pdf

Dear UnitedHealthcare Appeals Department,

I am appealing the denial of my prior authorization request for a total hip replacement (CPT 27130). My surgeon, Dr. Duval, has documented that this procedure is medically necessary for me, and I am asking the plan to reconsider its decision.

## Why I believe the denial should be reversed

The plan's own policy states: "Coverage Rationale Surgery of the hip and surgical treatment for Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) Syndrome is proven and medically necessary in certain circumstances." My records show I meet the kind of circumstances the policy contemplates as medically necessary, as explained below.

The policy also states: "For medical necessity clinical coverage criteria, refer to the InterQual® CP:" This tells me the actual clinical criteria used to evaluate my case are contained in InterQual, not fully spelled out in the denial notice itself.

I have noticed that most of the specific evidence discussed in my denial — the material about statistically significant differences in iHOT-33, HOOS, and EQ-VAS scores between arthroscopy and conservative treatment, and the language stating that "Surgical treatment for Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) Syndrome is unproven and not medically necessary in the presence of advanced osteoarthritis (i.e., Tönnis Grade 2 or 3) and/or severe cartilage damage (i.e., Outerbridge Grade III or IV)" — concerns hip **arthroscopy for FAI**, a different procedure than the one my surgeon requested. I am requesting total hip **replacement**, not arthroscopic FAI surgery, and I ask the plan to confirm that the correct clinical criteria for total hip replacement (rather than the FAI arthroscopy criteria quoted in my denial) were actually applied to my case.

To the extent the advanced-osteoarthritis language is relevant at all, my imaging supports rather than undermines the need for surgery. My weight-bearing AP pelvis radiograph from 2026-06-04 showed joint space narrowed to 1 mm superolaterally with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes — findings consistent with advanced degenerative joint disease, which is the condition that total hip replacement, as opposed to hip-preserving arthroscopy, is generally used to treat.

The policy further states: "Medical records documentation may be required to assess whether the member meets the clinical criteria for coverage but does not guarantee coverage of the service requested." I have provided the documentation below to support that my case meets the applicable criteria, understanding that this letter alone does not guarantee approval:

- **Symptom duration and severity:** 12 months of progressive hip pain unrelieved by rest.
- **Conservative treatment attempted and failed:** 8 weeks of supervised physical therapy (16 visits, 2026-05-13 to 2026-07-08) focused on hip abductor strengthening and gait, as documented in the physical therapy discharge note; NSAIDs for 6 months with inadequate relief; a corticosteroid injection on 2026-05-28 that gave only 3 weeks of partial relief.
- **Imaging findings:** joint space narrowed to 1 mm superolaterally with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes (2026-06-04).
- **Functional limitation:** I ambulate with a cane, am limited to walking one block, and cannot put on my shoes unassisted.
- **Exam findings:** positive provocative testing on the affected side, with range of motion limited by pain.
- **No disqualifying factors:** no active infection, no untreated substance use, BMI 29, non-smoker.

## Request for the criteria applied to my case

The denial notice states that InterQual® criteria were used, but InterQual is licensed software and its content was not included with my denial. Under ERISA and ACA appeal rules, I am entitled to receive, free of charge, the specific rule or criterion relied on for this determination. I am formally requesting, in writing, the InterQual subset, edition, and full criteria text applied to my determination, so that I and my surgeon can review it and respond specifically to whatever standard was actually used.

## What I am asking

I ask that UnitedHealthcare reconsider this denial in light of the documentation above, confirm which clinical criteria (InterQual subset and edition) were actually applied to a total hip replacement request, and provide that criteria text in writing. I understand my appeal must be received by 2027-01-27, and I am submitting it through member.uhc.com and/or by calling the number on my member ID card, as well as to the appeal address printed on my denial letter, [insert appeal mailing address from denial letter if provided separately].

Please let me know if any additional information is needed from me or from Dr. Duval's office to complete this review.

Sincerely,

______________________________
Morgan Iverson
Member ID: W702529422
Date: [insert date of signing]
Phone: [insert phone number]
Email: [insert email address]

---

*This letter is not medical or legal advice and does not guarantee that coverage will be approved.*

While conservative treatments such as physical therapy may yield comparable short-term outcomes, recent evidence suggests that arthroscopy provides superior results, particularly for younger patients and those without preoperative OA.

The authors stated that differences were statistically significant between arthroscopy and conservative treatment for Hip Outcome Score (HOOS) (follow-up for 6 months), iHOT-33 (follow-up for 6 months) improvement, iHOT-33 (follow-up for 12 months) improvement, iHOT-33 (follow-up for 12 months), EQ-5D-5L index score (follow-up for 12 months) and arthroscopic surgery showed higher benefits than conservative therapy.
Evidence of additional benefit of arthroscopic hip surgery against conservative therapy in the field of improving quality of life (three trials, 575 participants, ES = 2.109, 95% CI:

The authors included studies that directly compared surgical and nonsurgical treatment for symptomatic FAI and excluded those that did not use arthroscopic treatment as a surgical technique and studies performed on patients with concomitant diagnoses instead of pure FAI.

The authors compared clinical outcome scores at 6 and 12 months of follow-up for iHOT-33, HOOS, EuroQol-visual analog scale (EQ-VAS), modified Harris hip score (mHHS), and nonarthritic hip score (NAHS).

At 6 months of follow-up, the authors noted no statistically significant differences in iHOT-33 ratings [mean difference (MD) = 7.92, p = .15], HOOS (MD of HOOS-ADL = 5.15, p = .26 and MD of HOOS-Sports = 2.65, p = .79, respectively), and EQ-VAS (MD = 1.22, p = .76) between the two treatment strategies.

The authors concluded that despite arthroscopy being associated with significantly superior iHOT-33 scores after 12 months of follow-up, they were unable to discern the difference between the treatment strategies using other scoring methods, such as HOOS, EQ-VAS, mHHS, and NAHS.
Most studies adopted different physical therapy protocols, and some studies even combined injection therapy with nonsurgical treatment.
